answer.rationale:
The competitor's entry pricing creates pressure toward promotional_pricing, but memory_73 is the one inherited record that explicitly carries its own caveat: the +31% conversion / +18% revenue came with -12pp later-cycle retention and was labeled not repeatable for planning. Discounting into a price-sensitive SMB segment against a competitor who can go lower would buy conversions that decay, which is the opposite of the sustainable qualified-revenue objective. So I am not spending the single slot there, and I am not spending verification on it either, since the record already tells me what I need.

The two declining metrics are plausibly causally linked: onboarding completion down 4% is upstream of activation down 6%. Fixing the upstream funnel step is more likely to move both than messaging that nudges accounts already stuck in an incomplete onboarding flow. simplify_onboarding also has converging support from two independent records (memory_31 on signup field reduction, memory_86 on onboarding length), which is stronger than the single-record basis for activation_messaging. Referral incentives (memory_57) target established customers and do not address the funnel decline; enterprise_sales_assist (memory_44) is a different segment than the one under attack.

I am spending verification on memory_86 and memory_31 because they are the memories I intend to act on, and because their headline framing is exactly the shape that memory_73 warns about: completion rates, time-to-value, and first-week activation are all early-window metrics. memory_73 shows this organization has previously seen an early-window win invert at later cycle. I want the original records to tell me whether the 'durable lift' in memory_31 was actually measured past week one, and whether memory_86's adoption lift was ever tied to retained or qualified revenue rather than just funnel throughput. If the archive shows these were only ever measured in the early window, the consolidated summaries are overstating durability and my confidence should drop.

Downstream risk is real even if the memories check out: removing signup fields or onboarding steps can strip out qualification and intent signals, admitting lower-quality accounts that complete faster but convert worse. That is a mechanism by which a genuine completion lift produces flat or negative qualified revenue. So this runs as a standard experiment with holdout, instrumented on downstream qualified revenue and later-cycle retention, not on completion rate alone — completion is the proxy, not the goal. I am not treating the inherited summaries as settled enough for broad rollout.
